caption_used: Distribution of samples (%) across varying values of sample-level ambiguity standard deviation (outer ring) and sample-level maximum ambiguity (inner ring). The outer ring shows that nearly half of all samples (49.0%) exhibit zero ambiguity standard deviation (Std: 0.0), followed by Std: 0.47 at 38.0%, with the remaining samples distributed between Std: 0.82 at 7.0% and Std: 0.94 at 5.0%. In the inner ring, Max Ambiguity of 1 accounts for approximately 39.0% of samples, Max: 2 represents the largest inner-ring segment at 47.7%, and Max: 3 comprises 14.2%. The two rings together indicate that the majority of samples exhibit low ambiguity across both measures.
raw_response: This donut chart visually represents the distribution of samples as percentages, categorized by two interdependent variables: sample-level ambiguity standard deviation (outer ring) and sample-level maximum ambiguity (inner ring). The chart is composed of two concentric rings, with the outer ring divided into four segments representing different standard deviation values (Std: 0.0, Std: 0.47, Std: 0.82, Std: 0.94), and the inner ring divided into three segments representing different maximum ambiguity values (Max: 1, Max: 2, Max: 3). The outer ring segments are colored in varying shades of dark to medium blue, with the largest segment (Std: 0.0) at 49.0%, followed by Std: 0.47 at 38.0%, Std: 0.82 at 7.0%, and Std: 0.94 at 5.0%. The inner ring segments are colored in varying shades of light blue, with Max: 2 at 47.7%, Max: 1 at 39.0%, and Max: 3 at 14.2%. Each segment is labeled with its corresponding percentage value, and the chart includes two legends: one for the outer ring (Ambiguity Std) and one for the inner ring (Max Ambiguity), which map the colors to their respective categories. The segments are arranged in a clockwise order, with the largest segments positioned prominently in the upper left and lower right quadrants of the chart. There are no exploded or emphasized segments, and the chart does not include a combined legend or cross-tabulation of the two variables. The chart is designed to show the marginal distributions of each variable independently, rather than their joint distribution.
